arxiv:2611.34923.text: Mixture-of-Loops Transformer. From Lianghui Zhu and colleagues. Looped Transformers reuse layers to gain expressive power, but repeated passes can make them inefficient. Mixture-of-Loops Transformer uses attention keys and values as memory, letting later loops selectively reuse information while reducing dependence between loops. Its U-shaped design skips decoder passes that are not needed for predictions, and in large-scale training it improved token efficiency and several language-model benchmarks. At inference, it matched the latency of a Transformer without loops in the tested small models.

arxiv:2611.34232.text: OS-Omni: Benchmarking Generalist Computer-Using Agents on Long-Horizon Workflows Across Platforms. From Hui Shen and colleagues. Computer-using agents need to handle whole workflows across devices, but existing tests often focus on just one platform or short tasks. OS-Omni is a benchmark covering six platforms, with tasks that preserve application state and workflows linking a computer with an Android phone. Its tasks take far more interaction steps than earlier reference tasks, and the best tested agent succeeds less often than people overall. Performance varies sharply by platform, showing that reliable long workflows and lasting changes remain difficult.

arxiv:2611.34575.text: Sage-Med: Scaling Medical Multimodal Intelligence. From Med Team and colleagues. Medical multimodal models often lag behind general-purpose systems, especially in interpreting images, and simply making them larger does not close that gap. Sage-Med-Preview combines carefully selected medical data with a training program that moves from medical pretraining through supervised refinement and adaptive reinforcement learning. It scores 58.26 percent on 31 public multimodal benchmarks, outperforming the leading open-source medical model and a general scientific model. The results show that staged training can improve both medical image understanding and language skills, though complex reasoning remains difficult.

arxiv:2611.34907.text: Agentic LongLive: Asynchronous Agentic Memory for Long Video Generation. From Shaoteng Liu and colleagues. Live video generators can accept new prompts as a story unfolds, but they often lose track of people, objects, and places. Agentic LongLive adds a separate memory agent that updates text and images from prompts seen so far, then supplies that memory before each new shot without slowing the stream. On a new benchmark, it substantially improved consistency in persistent details, protagonist identity, and returning locations, while adding about one percent to generation time. It also streamed faster than real time and maintained image quality over fourteen-minute stories.

arxiv:2611.34237.text: VibeVideoAgent: Closing the Perceptual Loop for Code-Driven Video Generation. From Xuanyu Zheng and colleagues. Code-driven video can run without errors yet still contain unreadable text, awkward camera views, broken interactions, or out-of-sync narration. VibeVideoAgent lets coding agents inspect short previews as they work, using separate, brief perception sessions and compact findings instead of loading full renders into the coding session. Across all two hundred thirty-nine benchmark tasks, it improved overall audiovisual quality for three coding agents, with the largest gains in audio and video synchronization. Tests also found that each component contributed, and that the size of code edits shaped the balance between meeting requirements and perceptual quality.

arxiv:2611.34941.text: Improving and Expanding Video Editing Capabilities Without Videos. From Ji Xie and colleagues. Video editors have fewer editing skills than image editors, partly because training them requires matched pairs of original and edited videos. Image-to-Video Transfer teaches a pretrained video editor by having it edit single images as if they were one-frame videos, guided by an image editor, with no new videos or changes to the model design. At test time, the upgraded editor can apply these skills to full clips while keeping motion consistent. Tests with three video editors show stronger existing skills and new ones, with top results on two video-editing benchmarks.

arxiv:2611.34457.text: ProxyGenBench: Benchmarking Proxy-Guided Video Generation. From Zhenchen Tang and colleagues. Controlling how generated video scenes unfold is difficult, especially when guides are rough and leave details open. ProxyGenBench tests how well video generators use animated three-dimensional blockouts while preserving their structure, filling in missing content, correcting artifacts, and matching text, images, and sound to the right events. It evaluates five generators across varied scenes and input conditions. The results show that proxies improve control over space and motion, but more detail can hurt completion, and following the structure does not guarantee correct matching.

arxiv:2611.34290.text: StateWeaver: Multi-Agent Coordination of Story-State Transitions for Long-Horizon Video Generation. From Modi Jin and colleagues. Long video generators often lose consistency between shots and struggle to show changes in a story accurately. StateWeaver coordinates agents that review clips, update visual references when details need repair, and carry confirmed character and scene states into later shots. It also separates work by task and repair round, keeping planning and fixes from accumulating in one context. Across multiple benchmarks, it outperforms existing methods and maintains consistency in long videos with both predefined and autonomously planned storyboards.

arxiv:2611.34420.text: DocSEAM: Bidirectional Cross-Page Encoding for Multi-Page Document Understanding. From Hoang-Nhat Nguyen and colleagues. Multi-page document models often encode each page on its own, so information can be lost at page boundaries. DocSEAM adds a lightweight step that lets each page draw on nearby pages, while keeping the number of visual tokens unchanged. After training, a nine-billion-parameter model achieved the best results among evaluated open-weight models of up to ten billion parameters on five document question-answering benchmarks. It also proved less sensitive to where pages were split and improved the location of answers spanning pages.

arxiv:2611.34128.text: FoundSurface: Feedforward Ray-Based 3D Scene Surface Reconstruction from Unposed Images. From Shenxing Wei and colleagues. Reconstructing accurate surfaces from images without known camera poses is difficult, and point-based methods often leave the result sparse. FoundSurface combines geometric clues from a pre-trained pointmap model with selected reference views, then uses image rays to estimate continuous surfaces and fine details. Trained across nine datasets, it generalizes to six unseen datasets and surpasses leading methods in geometric accuracy and detail preservation.

arxiv:2611.34813.text: Solve Vision with Code: Coding Agents Are Stronger Visual Reasoners Than Video Models. From Dezhi Luo and colleagues. Visual reasoning tests ask models to turn a starting image and a prompt into a video that shows a task being completed. This work compares video generators with coding agents, which write programs to render the answer, using the same inputs and a rule-based evaluator. On a five-hundred-task benchmark, the three strongest closed-model agents scored above zero point eight nine, more than zero point two two higher than the best video model. The results suggest that for tasks computable from an image and prompt, writing code is currently a more reliable route than generating video.

arxiv:2611.34811.text: HOG-WAM: Improving Visual Robustness through Future Gradient Prediction. From Boxuan Dong and colleagues. Visual corruption can disrupt world-action models, which predict future observations and actions to guide control. HOG-WAM adds a training-only module that predicts future image structure from demonstration images, helping shape the visual features used for control while keeping the same image-to-action design at deployment. It achieves the highest success among compared policies across four tested corruptions, and improves results on simulated and physical tasks. The gains are larger on physical tasks, including under noisy observations.

arxiv:2611.34051.text: Stable Gated DeltaNet-2: Understanding and Mitigating Recurrent State Instability. From Xichong Zhang and colleagues. Long-context training can make recurrent states in Gated DeltaNet-2 grow exponentially, even when the model is not writing new information. The work traces this instability to an imbalance in how the model reads and erases information, then proposes symmetric erasure and controlled residual writing. The design limits state growth while keeping chunkwise parallel computation. In experiments, it trains stably and improves long-context retrieval and accuracy across downstream tasks.

arxiv:2611.34147.text: Letting Models Manage Their Own Context: Where We Stand. From Alessio Devoto and colleagues. As conversations fill a model's context window, agent systems usually summarize the history automatically. This study tests a different approach, giving models a tool to choose what to compact and when, across research and engineering tasks with context budgets from eight thousand to five hundred twelve thousand tokens. Models that used the tool well often scored higher with fewer input tokens; one model nearly tripled its score at a tight budget. Reusing cached information also cut processing compute by up to fifteen percent without measurable accuracy loss.

arxiv:2611.34852.text: DRBench Pro: A Knowledge-Centric Benchmark for Professional Deep Research Agents. From Han Huang and colleagues. Deep research agents can produce polished reports while missing major lines of inquiry or exploring them only superficially, and current benchmarks do not measure this knowledge coverage directly. DRBench Pro builds structured knowledge maps from Wikipedia and uses them to create research questions and evidence-based scoring rules. Across 144 cases in 24 domains, it found clear differences in agents' breadth and depth, while the top agent reached 57.04 percent overall coverage. Its automated judgments closely matched human ratings.

arxiv:2611.34849.text: Real2SimLab: A Unified Platform for Real-to-Simulation Transfer. From Yongchang Zhang and colleagues. Evaluating tools that turn real-world video into simulations is difficult because each benchmark requires its own setup, creating many separate integrations. Real2SimLab offers one platform that runs a method's simulation program and scores it with each benchmark's original scoring system. It also creates training examples and reward labels while filtering out benchmark videos to avoid data contamination. The platform supports 47 coding agents, five other methods, and six benchmarks, alongside a research map of nearly 300 papers.

arxiv:2611.34929.text: High-Fidelity Image Matting with Pixel-Space Diffusion Transformers. From Baihan Yang and colleagues. Image matting needs precise edges and opacity, but latent diffusion can lose fine detail through compression and reconstruction. PixelMatte adapts pretrained pixel-space diffusion transformers, feeding the image, a trimap, and a noisy matte together, and predicts the result in one pass. It works even with a model trained only for text-to-image, using synthetic supervision, real-image fine-tuning, and two small calibration modules. Across four benchmarks, it substantially improves on RenderMatte, reducing opacity and gradient errors by twenty-four to forty-four percent on two benchmarks.

arxiv:2611.34466.text: EgoUseBench: Benchmarking Computer-Use Agents under Evolving First-Person Contexts. From Yurun Chen and colleagues. Smart glasses can give computer agents clues from a user's surroundings, but those clues may be incomplete or change as the user acts. EgoUseBench tests whether agents can keep digital tasks aligned with what users are doing and want. It includes six hundred and ninety-three tasks based on more than seventy-four hours of first-person recordings, with settings ranging from explicit instructions to continuous observations. In the online setting, agents' average success rates were 26.3 percent lower than in computer-use tasks with explicit instructions.

arxiv:2611.34693.text: ShowNow: Fine-Grained Speculative Streaming for Responsive World Models. From Yiren Song and colleagues. Interactive world models need to keep generating video while reacting quickly to user actions, but large generation blocks can delay responses. ShowNow uses spare computation during playback to prepare several possible futures before an action arrives, then commits to video in small steps. On one H100, its five-billion-parameter model generates at four hundred and eighty-pixel resolution, sixteen frames per second, while preparing eight futures. In ViZDoom, it cuts median input-to-display latency from six hundred and twenty to two hundred and eight milliseconds, though visual fidelity and long-term consistency involve trade-offs.

arxiv:2611.33636.text: What Is Redundant at High Resolution? Efficient Attention and Feed-Forward Design for All-in-One Image Restoration. From Dongheon Lee and colleagues. All-in-one image restoration must handle large, high-resolution feature maps, which can make processing slow and memory-intensive. HiGLR examines where attention and feed-forward networks repeat unnecessary work, then redesigns both to reduce that cost. It uses a learned kernel at the finest scale, shares routing across nearby queries at intermediate scales, and separates compact spatial mixing from expanded feature processing. The resulting network reaches state-of-the-art performance, with inference up to four point two four times faster than existing methods.

arxiv:2611.34452.text: Global Convergence of Second-Order Methods for Physics-Informed Neural Networks in the Overparameterized Limit. From Konstantin Riedl and colleagues. Second-order optimizers are increasingly used to train neural networks that solve partial differential equations, but their convergence has lacked a theory. This work analyzes regularized Newton and Gauss-Newton training as the network grows wider. It shows that the dynamics approach a deterministic limit, the equation residual vanishes, and under mild assumptions the network converges to the PDE solution. With sufficiently small regularization, leading residual components decay exponentially, while regularization also reduces the slowdown of high-frequency components that affects gradient descent.

arxiv:2611.34835.text: Full Structure Recovery of Linearized Reed-Solomon Codes. From Valentina Astore and colleagues. Linearized Reed-Solomon codes have strong decoding properties, but their structure may make them vulnerable in code-based cryptography. Earlier methods for identifying that structure either covered only some cases or required too much computation. This work gives a polynomial-time method to recover the full structure using only an arbitrary generator matrix, combining attack techniques with matrix operations and shortening. The results show these codes cannot be used as they are for encryption schemes modeled on McEliece.

arxiv:2611.34921.text: Bound Entanglement with Negative Partial Transpose Exists. From Islam Faisal. Whether a state with a negative partial transpose can still be impossible to distill has been a key question in quantum information. This work gives an example: a Werner state on two eight-dimensional systems has a negative partial transpose, yet no local operations and classical communication protocol can extract entanglement from any number of copies. Even allowing separable operations, its two-qubit output cannot exceed a fidelity of about zero point six zero four with a Bell state. The result also shows that distillable entanglement is neither additive nor convex.

arxiv:2611.34039.text: Asymptotically Efficient Finite Impulse Response System Identification without Noise Knowledge. From Zichen Liu and colleagues. Estimating a system's response from its inputs is difficult when measurement noise is unknown or contains extreme values. This work introduces two adaptive methods that estimate the noise distribution from the data, then use it to refine the system estimate without assuming a particular noise model. The methods are shown to be consistent and asymptotically efficient, reaching the theoretical precision limit under mild conditions. Simulations find they are more robust and accurate than least squares and least absolute deviations, often matching methods given the true noise distribution.

arxiv:2611.33318.text: What Must LLM Agents Communicate? From Information Loss to Communication Failures. From Yi-Yun Chu and colleagues. Teams of language model agents can hold all the evidence needed for a decision and still make poor predictions. This work studies what information they need to share, how they should choose relevant evidence, and whether they use what they receive. In controlled experiments, local probability reports often lose essential information, and the predicted loss closely matches the observed drop in performance. Asking questions first can help when evidence depends on a private query, but even sufficient messages may be selected or used incorrectly.

arxiv:2611.34809.text: PrO Filtering via Kernel Mean Embedding Dynamics. From Linfeng Wang and colleagues. Filtering with a flawed model can become overconfident, and Gaussian filters may struggle when observations conflict with forecasts. This work develops a particle-based version of predictively oriented filtering, which can preserve probability near both the forecast and the observation. It uses kernel mean embedding dynamics to transport samples, without needing importance weights or the predictive density. Tests on difficult nonlinear examples show substantial improvement over the Gaussian version, while the required number of transport steps does not increase for unusually surprising observations.

arxiv:2611.34807.text: On the Distance Properties of Huffman Sequences. From Parker Huggins and colleagues. Designing codes with a fixed autocorrelation requires understanding how far apart the sequences can be. This work studies pairwise distances between sequences that share the same aperiodic autocorrelation, and shows that those distances are set by a signed pattern describing how their spectral zeros differ. For Huffman sequences, rotating or reflecting the zeros preserves pairwise distance, and the study also gives lower bounds on the minimum distance. These results can help guide code design for integrated sensing and communication.

arxiv:2611.34363.text: Single-Database Rewards Are Hackable: Counterfactual Execution for Trustworthy Text-to-SQL RL. From Shreshth Rai and colleagues. Text-to-SQL systems can earn a reward for a wrong query when the database happens to lack rows that reveal its mistake. This work tests a counterfactual reward that also runs each query on hidden, generated copies of the database. On synthetic audit questions, the strict version cut fully rewarded buggy queries from twenty-nine point five percent to sixteen point eight percent, and reward hacks from fifty-four point one percent to one point nine percent, without rejecting any correct queries. In training tests, the mean version did not improve in-domain accuracy, but gained one point six points on Spider; results also varied across seeds.

arxiv:2611.33925.text: Beyond the Happy Path: Generalizing Robot World Models from Simulated Failures. From Zhiyue Zhao and colleagues. Robot world models often learn from successful demonstrations, so they can mispredict what happens when a grasp slips or pushes an object. WorldReforge trains them on sixty-two thousand simulated trajectories made by perturbing grasps, with labels for object motion, contact, and surface points. On Cosmos three Nano, it cuts object trajectory error by twenty-eight point two percent overall and thirty-five percent on unseen objects, and improves predictions of how action outcomes diverge. It also improves reconstruction on real failure videos, showing that simulated mistakes can teach useful physics.

arxiv:2611.34314.text: Variational Principles and Machine Learning: a Numerical Analysis and PDE perspective. From Charalambos G. Makridakis. Machine learning often relies on large minimisation problems, but the mathematical ideas that explain their reliability are not always clear. These notes view machine learning through variational principles and numerical analysis, examining how ideas such as stability, consistency, and approximation apply to neural networks. They show how the variational structure of a continuous problem can shape neural-network approximations. The framework also suggests that alternative, strongly coercive principles may lead to more stable, reliable, and potentially more efficient methods.

arxiv:2611.33227.text: Real Package, Wrong Controller: Static Auditing of Vendor, Protocol Mismatches in LLM-Generated PLC Code. From S M Zia Ur Rashid and colleagues. Generated industrial control code may use valid packages that still do not fit the declared controller or protocol. Proteus-OT checks this mismatch by comparing imports with a version-pinned graph of documented vendor bindings. Across eight hundred and eighty-three generated scripts, it finds mismatches in twenty point four percent; among scripts with an adjudicable human label, none of twenty-eight human files has one, though that sample is too small to estimate prevalence. The results show that package existence alone can miss real compatibility problems, while repository-based authorship classification should not be mistaken for proof of who wrote the code.

arxiv:2611.33270.text: Sharp one-shot bounds and optimal exponents of universal randomness extraction. From Bartosz Regula and colleagues. Quantum privacy amplification needs sharp limits on how well a secret key can be extracted when an adversary holds quantum information. This work connects extraction errors to constrained hypothesis tests and derives matching bounds for universal hash functions in several regimes. It shows that a known leftover hash bound is tight up to a constant factor for strongly four-universal hashing. The results also determine exact error exponents in the strong converse regime for two-universal hashing.

arxiv:2611.33593.text: Optimization of a Hybrid Solar-Biogas-Battery Energy Storage Microgrid: A Case Study. From John Elomunait and colleagues. Unreliable grid power limits access to electricity in low-income regions, including eastern Uganda. This study optimizes a microgrid for Soroti, combining concentrating solar power with heat storage, biogas generation, and batteries, using six years of weather data. The selected design produces sixty-one point three gigawatt-hours a year and exports twenty-eight point eight gigawatt-hours. It also cuts costs by thirty-two point two percent compared with grid-only supply, suggesting this approach could support wider electricity access.

arxiv:2611.34158.text: Strategic and Robust Task Allocation for Combat Objectives in Adversarial Multi-Agent Environments. From Jonas Peché and colleagues. Assigning several agents to objectives in a contested game is difficult because teams must account for uncertainty, travel, and changing opponent behavior. This system predicts tactical signals for each agent, then combines them with rules and uses a flow solver to make coordinated assignments subject to game constraints. Learning is limited to the tactical estimates, keeping the assignments easier to inspect and control. Tests indicate the approach can produce stable, feasible allocations within strict real-time limits, though it remains a research prototype.

arxiv:2611.33892.text: Certifying a Sufficient Gaussian Dependence Regime for Learned Weighted FDR Control. From Soyeong Oh. Learned weights can make multiple testing more powerful, but their dependence on one another can undermine false discovery rate control, even when they are independent of the tests. This work uses reference observations to check whether the dependence among weights is safe enough for weighted Benjamini-Hochberg, and otherwise switches to a prespecified fallback. Under stated conditions, the procedure controls the false discovery rate across the allowed Gaussian dependence patterns. The study also gives limits on how much data certification needs and shows how testing subjects can provide certification data in some settings.

arxiv:2611.34550.text: An Information-Theoretic Analysis of Information Hiding in Semantic Communication. From Yanhao Huo and colleagues. Semantic communication aims to preserve meaning rather than reproduce every transmitted symbol, but information hiding at this level has lacked a systematic theory. This work builds a framework linking semantic and ordinary signals, with separate limits on changes to the signal and its meaning. It expresses hiding capacity as a contest between a hider and an observer, and establishes the result using coding and decoding arguments. The analysis shows semantic hiding is not always better than classical hiding, and that grouping distinct signals under the same meaning can reduce capacity.

arxiv:2611.34777.text: When Every Rollout Fails: Splicing Learner-Conditioned Options into Long-Horizon Agent RL. From Haowen Hou and colleagues. Long-horizon agent tasks can leave reinforcement learning without a useful learning signal when every sampled attempt fails. SPLICE finds promising local actions in failed attempts: a proposal model suggests short options, then current-policy continuations estimate their value. The method uses the better options as training targets rather than supplying complete solutions. Across two tasks and two policy families, SPLICE beat standard training and full-solution guidance in all four settings, with gains of two point eight to nine point eight percentage points.

arxiv:2611.34675.text: RoboEvosquared: Recursive Robot Self-Improvement via Harness-Policy Co-Evolution. From Chenzhi Liu and colleagues. Robots can struggle in unfamiliar settings, while reasoning agents can find solutions but often spend too much time deliberating and repairing mistakes. RoboEvo squared lets robot policies and software tools improve each other: failures guide the tools to find reusable solutions, and successful attempts train the policy to choose better actions. Without new human demonstrations, it raises hybrid success on LIBERO-PRO from 30.4 percent to 90.5 percent, showing how repeated practice can make robots both more capable and more efficient.

arxiv:2611.34068.text: Budget, Readout or Reasoning? Where Small Reasoning Models Lose Value in Auction Bidding. From Mahbod Khaleti and colleagues. Choosing a bid from a win-probability curve should be a straightforward calculation, but reasoning models can still lose value even when given the needed estimates. Across six models and two auction settings, wrong bids usually favored the highest available bid, while arithmetic mistakes were rare. Short token limits and leaving the reasoning block open also hurt performance. Letting models finish and checking bids against their own reasoning recovered most or all of the value lost to the calculator's bids.

arxiv:2611.34331.text: Puzzling-Bench: Evaluating Language Models on 23,777 Human-Written Puzzles with Community-Verified Answers. From Abhinav Sharma and colleagues. Language models can solve many puzzles, but comparing their abilities is difficult when answers are unclear or data may have leaked into training. Puzzling-Bench brings together 23,777 puzzles with answers verified by the community, along with hints, categories, and images for about a third. Across nine models, the best scored 74.8 percent on a shared set, while 17 puzzles stumped every model. Hiding images sharply reduced scores for the two strongest models, showing how much visual clues can matter.
